John Howe
JON HOW
proper noun (person)
English Puritan minister (1630-1705), domestic chaplain to Oliver Cromwell, author of The Living Temple and The Blessedness of the Righteous.

📖 Biblical Definition

John Howe was an English Puritan minister of unusual breadth and elevation of mind, who served for a time as domestic chaplain to Oliver Cromwell and, after the Restoration and his ejection, ministered among the nonconformists with a notably catholic and peaceable spirit. His most famous work, The Living Temple, argues from the nature of God and man that the human soul was made to be the dwelling-place of God, ruined by sin yet destined to be restored as God's temple through redemption. Other works, such as The Blessedness of the Righteous and On Delighting in God, breathe the same air of lofty, reverent meditation on the greatness and goodness of God and the soul's chief end in communion with Him. Howe combined deep learning with a warm, contemplative piety, and labored for unity among the godly across party lines without surrendering the substance of the Reformed faith. He stands in the dictionary as the Puritan of magnanimous spirit and elevated devotion, who taught the church that man was made for God, that sin has unhoused the divine Guest, and that grace rebuilds the soul into a living temple for the glory of its Maker.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

English Puritan minister (1630-1705), chaplain to Cromwell, author of The Living Temple; a man of broad learning, catholic spirit, and elevated devotion who taught that the soul was made to be the dwelling-place of God.

JOHN HOWE, proper noun. English Puritan minister (1630-1705).

Domestic chaplain to Oliver Cromwell; ejected after the Restoration.

Author of The Living Temple, The Blessedness of the Righteous, and On Delighting in God.

Known for breadth of learning, catholic spirit, and contemplative piety.

Taught that the soul was made to be the temple of the living God.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Cor 3:16 — "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?"

John 14:23 — "Jesus answered and said unto him, If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him."

2 Cor 6:16 — "And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols? for ye are the temple of the living God; as God hath said, I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people."

Psa 73:25 — "Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Howe's vision is honored by recovering the truth that man was made for communion with God as His temple, against a secular anthropology that reduces the human person to matter, appetite, or self-definition.

expand to see more

Reductive-anthropology misreading. The modern world defines man as a clever animal, a bundle of needs, or a self-made identity, with no Maker and no end beyond himself. Howe's Living Temple answers from the nature of things: man was framed to house the presence of God, and only in that indwelling communion is he whole. The dictionary holds the high biblical doctrine of man — made in God's image for God's fellowship, ruined by sin, restored in Christ — against every account that empties the human person of its God-ward purpose.

This entry faces little direct postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the soul's chief end. Howe's lofty devotion fixed on the greatness and goodness of God as the one worthy object of the heart. In an age of distraction and self-absorption, the dictionary commends his example of elevated, God-centered meditation, and his conviction that the restless human soul finds rest only when God again dwells within His temple.
